text: 2 4.3.1.1 Safety Codes and Standards Section 2.8 of NLR’s 2025 Hydrogen Infrastructure Analysis Frameworks for Aviation Applications report details the applicable safety codes and standards for hydrogen handling and accompanying equipment at airports. The most comprehensive standard for hydrogen utilization is NFPA 2, Hydrogen Technologies Code, which covers safety and design (including setback distances) for several types of hydrogen equipment including bulk liquid and gaseous storage, fuel cells, and hydrogen generation systems (NFPA 2026a). In terms of hydrogen refueling procedures, no standards have been developed for liquid hydrogen dispensing into aircraft as of 2025. Further research and development are needed in this area before these regulations can be developed effectively. Existing safety codes and regulations regarding hydrogen-powered aircraft technology are also not comprehensive and require updating once more knowledge is gained on how to operate the technology with all safety concerns mitigated (Bracci et al. 2026). 4.3.1.2 Infrastructure Spatial Footprint Notably, NFPA 2 provides guidance on the necessary offset distances for bulk liquid hydrogen storage from surrounding infrastructure. Offset distances vary by exposure group, with the largest offset distances required for lot lines, air intakes, building openings, and ignition sources (Exposure Group 1). Definitions of each exposure group are found in Table 8.3.2.3.1.6(a) of NFPA 2. Of note, airport ground support equipment, parked aircraft, and jet fuel storage tanks would likely fall in Exposure Group 2. However, NFPA 2 does not call out these infrastructure components specifically, so further regulatory clarification is necessary. Table 8.3.2.3.1.6(b) provides additional offset distances for each exposure group with different inner diameter piping. Figure 43 provides an example of the estimated spatial footprint for a 4,500-kg bulk LH storage system that meets 2 offset distance requirements in NFPA 2. This storage tank volume is roughly equivalent to the onboard storage volume of five LH -powered regional turboprop aircraft (see Table 11). (2026) As LH storage requirements at an airport exceed 4,500 kg, system designers should look to 2 place more storage tanks in a manner that minimizes the additional spatial footprint (i.e., placing storage tanks side by side). One method to reduce total area required for storage is to surround the storage system with a fire barrier wall.
